runs.text: Vocabulary with a precise meaning in rc-git. Definitions stand on their own; the code implements them, not the other way around.

The single decision-and-write path for every mutation rc-git performs. Nothing else in the project may change a repository or talk to the network; a feature that needs either asks the guard's policy first and runs the action inside it. rc-git runs no
process for repository operations; only the in-app updater runs
The policy's answer is allow, confirm (with a challenge), or deny — and a deny is final inside rc-git: the message points the user at git itself rather than offering a way through.

What the user must do before a risky action runs: at minimum press a confirm button, and for most destructive actions also type an exact phrase (usually the name of the thing being destroyed). Some confirm-only actions are destructive too: discarding working changes asks for the button alone, though nothing keeps the bytes it removes. In the CLI the button is an explicit
, and a confirm-only action refuses to run without it. Verifying a challenge is the only way to obtain the proof the write path demands, so an unconfirmed action cannot be expressed.

A ref recorded under rc-git's own namespace before a destructive action runs, pointing at whatever is about to be deleted, so the previous state can be restored by hand. Backups are numbered rather than overwritten, so repeating an action never destroys an earlier backup.

The paths an action is about to write that the working tree or the index has already changed. Any dirty overlap refuses the whole action before a single byte is written, and the refusal names the first such path, so uncommitted work is never overwritten and never partially applied. Paths the action does not touch are left alone, changes and all.

An action that moves the working tree to another commit — a fast-forward pull, a branch switch — decides this in a fixed order: plan the per-path changes, check them all for overlap, write the files, and move the ref last. The ordering is what keeps an interruption legible: it leaves visibly modified files on the commit the user started from, never something that reads as lost work. A stash restore refuses on overlap the same way, by its own route, and moves no ref.

One colored region of a file: a half-open byte range plus a class naming what the region means. A file's spans are ordered by start and never overlap — nested captures flatten to the innermost one — because the view applies exactly one color per range. A producer that combines several grammar layers, as markdown does for its inline prose and fenced code, must re-impose this contract before the spans leave the highlighter.

A region of a source file that leads to another module: the specifier of an import, a name the import binds, or a JSX element named after one. A link carries two byte ranges of the file and nothing else — the region to click and the specifier as written — so it never holds a path, and what it leads to is decided when it is followed, against the tree on screen at that moment.
Links match names by spelling. A local that shadows an import is linked like the import; telling them apart needs scope analysis the viewer does not do.
The markdown preview's document model. A
is one stretch of inline text that shares a single appearance — a style set, and at most one link — and concatenating a block's runs reproduces exactly what the reader sees. A
is one paragraph, heading, code block, table, or list item, carrying its runs plus the depth it sits at.

Blocks are flat, never a tree: nesting is two integers, a quote depth and a list depth, so a renderer indents from them rather than recursing, and a whole file is one array. Parsing produces blocks and runs and nothing else; deciding how either looks is the renderer's, and the renderer never re-reads the source.
An entry the file lists leave out until the user asks to see hidden files: version-control metadata and operating-system clutter such as
, named in one fixed list and matched by name at any depth, so everything inside a hidden folder is hidden with it.
Hidden is not ignored. A gitignored file like

is one the user may well want to read, so it stays visible, marked as ignored; and a hidden file is hidden whether git tracks it or not. The one exception is a change the user made: a tracked hidden file that changed stays in the change list, since hiding it would hide an edit. An untracked hidden file does not, so it can never ride along in a commit the user did not see.

How every repository is opened: only the repository's own configuration is read — no global or system git config, no environment variables, no include directives. Nor can that config aim rc-git at files outside the repository: a
that resolves anywhere but the opened directory is refused at open, and the repository's own
is never read. The one outside pointer followed is
, which lends objects from another repository read-only, as

relies on. A side effect: anything the repository's own config does not provide (an identity for reflog lines, credentials for a remote) must be supplied by rc-git itself per operation. What only the user's own config holds — a preferred pull strategy, a commit identity, a signing setup — is invisible to rc-git: it asks for an identity where one is needed, writes its commits unsigned, and never picks rebase or merge for a pull. The identity it asks for is a fallback saved for that one repository (Repository > Commit Identity… shows, edits or clears it; the defaults key is
), and a repository whose own config sets
always commits as that. The one thing read from outside the repository is the global ignore file at git's default location (
), so a file the user ignores globally does not show as untracked; a

The guard's network actions: fetch, fast-forward pull, plain push, and their sync composition. They speak HTTPS and SSH, both in-process so no child process is ever spawned, and are never force: a push the remote would have to discard history to accept is refused before anything is sent. A pull is the mirror case: when the branch and its upstream have both moved (diverged), it is refused with the counts on each side, and reconciling — rebase or merge — is left to git. Credentials are per-host, supplied by the caller per call, and never stored by the core.
A branch's upstream is the remote and branch its own config names. When the config names none — a branch pushed without setting one — rc-git takes the same-named branch on
, and the ahead/behind counts and pull compare against it. Push picks its remote the way git does —
, then the upstream's remote — and sends to that remote's
when it has one. It uploads only to the same-named branch, as git's
does, and when it pushes to the upstream's remote it refuses a branch whose config names an upstream under another name, so what push uploads to is always what the counts and pull compare against.

is a bare URL rather than a remote's name can be pushed, but not fetched or pulled: with no remote there are no fetch refspecs and no remote-tracking ref to read. Fetch and pull refuse it with a message that names the URL and says to add a named remote (
) and point the branch at it.

Every one of them ends. The app carries a cancel flag into the call that the user can raise from the other side while the transfer holds the thread, and each transport keeps an idle budget — the gap it tolerates between bytes, not the length of the transfer, so a slow link is never punished and a dead one does not wait forever. A cancelled operation stops between steps and leaves nothing half-applied.
How an SSH server proves its identity to rc-git. The

, then the system files) are consulted read-only and never written; a host they do not know is refused until the user approves the offered key's fingerprint, and that approval is remembered by the app itself, per host.

A key that contradicts an earlier in-app approval is refused the same way, without the trust sheet: a changed key is never treated as first contact. When the change is a legitimate rotation, the user removes the host's approval in Settings (Approved SSH Host Keys); the next fetch then meets the new key as unknown and asks again.

entry for the host, is refused with no way to approve it inside rc-git — like a guard deny, the message points the user at ssh itself. Lookup is keyed by the name actually dialed, so a config alias shares the trust of the real host behind it — unless the config sets
, which is looked up in its place, bare, as OpenSSH does.

What the user includes in the next commit or stash. Every changed file starts ticked, and an untick survives a rescan by path rather than by position. A tick is whole-file by default; a file whose hunks are ticked individually carries only those hunks, and ticking every hunk collapses back to a whole-file tick while unticking the last one unticks the file. A row that stands for several files — a folder in the change list — is ticked when all of them are, mixed when only some are, and one click moves the whole set.

The checks a self-update runs before it touches anything: the login shell must find the build's tools, and the checkout must be readable — plus, for a release update, free of uncommitted tracked changes. Both halves run outside the process, so both are bounded and both are logged before they run: a preflight that cannot answer fails with a reason rather than leaving the window spinning on one line.

What a self-update passes to the build that replaces it: the open tabs, in on-screen order, with the selected one. It is a handover rather than a save because both processes are alive at once — the new build reads the state while the old one is still running, so the write is flushed before the launch and the old process stops writing afterwards. The state is scoped by bundle identifier, which is why the identifier never depends on a version or a build number.

One place the back/forward list can return to: a tab, the pane it shows, and where its browser is — the tree it browses, the open file, what the history lists, and the commit in the detail. A stop names those things and holds none of them, so returning to one reads the repository as it is then: a ref that moved shows its new tip, and a file that is gone leaves the pane empty.

The list is one for the whole app, so a step back can cross from one repository to another. A move to where the list already is records nothing, and a move somewhere new drops the stops ahead. Only a change records a stop: when returning to one falls short, because what it names is gone, the list keeps its place and the screen is not recorded in its stead. Stops live in memory only, and closing a tab drops the ones that name it.
